analysis.one_liner: Strips federal tax breaks, royalty discounts, and financing subsidies from coal, oil, and gas producers.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 22 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to nine House committees and has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill strips away a long list of federal subsidies for coal, oil, and natural gas companies. It repeals tax deductions and credits the industry uses, raises the royalty rates energy companies pay to drill on federal land and offshore waters, lifts caps on what companies owe after oil spills, and bars federal agencies from financing fossil fuel projects at home and abroad. It would also restore an EPA fee on methane leaks and fund coal miners' black lung benefits through a higher coal excise tax.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers gain because the federal government would stop giving away billions in tax breaks, royalty relief, and loan guarantees to oil, gas, and coal companies. Coal miners gain from a larger Black Lung Disability Trust Fund paid by coal producers. People living near coasts, pipelines, and drilling sites gain from higher royalty rates, unlimited spill liability, and a restored EPA fee on methane leaks. Renewable energy producers gain from a hydrogen tax credit rewritten to reward only hydrogen made with wind, solar, geothermal, or hydropower.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals a long list of tax benefits for fossil fuel companies, including enhanced oil recovery credits, percentage depletion for coal, intangible drilling cost expensing, and LIFO inventory accounting for oil, gas, and coal firms
Raises federal royalty rates on coal, oil, and gas extracted from public lands and offshore waters from roughly 12.5% to 18.75%, so taxpayers get more for resources they own
Removes statutory liability caps for offshore facilities and pipelines, so companies responsible for oil spills — including tar sands pipeline spills — pay the full cost of damages
Raises the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund financing rate to 10 cents a barrel and denies tax deductions for oil spill removal costs and damages
Increases the coal excise tax from $1.10 to $1.38 per ton to shore up the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund that pays benefits to coal miners disabled by mining
Bars the Export-Import Bank, the Development Finance Corporation, and international financial institutions from using U.S. funds to support fossil fuel projects abroad
Restores the EPA rule charging oil and gas operators for wasted methane emissions by repealing the law that voided it
Repeals fossil fuel provisions of the 2025 tax law, including the new metallurgical coal production credit and expanded drilling tax breaks

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers and coal companies pay through lost tax deductions and credits, higher federal royalty rates, a new 13% tax on Gulf of Mexico offshore production, higher excise taxes, and expanded liability for spills. Some of these costs could be passed through to consumers in the form of somewhat higher fuel and utility prices.

drawbacks.text: Removing subsidies could raise production costs that oil, gas, and coal companies pass through to consumers in higher fuel and utility bills, hitting working households hardest
The new 13% severance tax on Gulf of Mexico offshore production and higher royalty rates could reduce domestic drilling activity, affecting energy-producing regions and jobs
The bill's hundreds of pages of tax-code changes would take years to administer and would face intense litigation over effective dates and contract grandfathering
Repealing the carbon oxide sequestration credit removes a subsidy that some climate advocates support for decarbonizing heavy industry, not just for oil recovery

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and concrete: ending roughly a century of tax and royalty preferences for some of the most profitable companies in the country, making polluters pay for spills and methane leaks, and shoring up black lung benefits for miners. The main costs are uncertain and diffuse — some subsidy repeal could reach consumers through energy prices, and drilling-dependent communities would bear adjustment costs. On balance the bill shifts costs from taxpayers onto the industries that profit from public resources, but with real transition risks for energy-heavy households and regions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sits with nine House committees, none of which has scheduled a hearing or vote since it was referred in July 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 23, 2025, with 22 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support
It was referred the same day to nine House committees, including Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources
No committee has taken further action — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record
Because Republicans control the House and every committee of referral, the bill cannot advance without majority-party scheduling, which has not occurred

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and coal companies are better off so far: their federal tax breaks, royalty rates, liability caps, and access to federal financing all remain unchanged because the bill has not moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies keep their subsidies

for.name: Rep. Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 22 Democratic cosponsors

for.name: Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 22 are Democrats, including Reps. Jayapal, Ocasio-Cortez, Khanna, Tlaib, and Schakowsky

against.name: House Republican committee chairs
against.role: House Republican majority and committee chairs
against.what_they_did: Hold the chairmanship of every committee the bill was referred to; no hearing or markup has been scheduled since the July 2025 referral

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors are Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republican support appears in the record, and Republicans control all nine committees the bill was referred to.

industries.note: The bill's central target: it repeals the industry's deductions, credits, accounting methods, and royalty relief. Industry interests run against the public's here — the subsidies the industry keeps are revenue taxpayers forgo.

Loses percentage depletion, capital-gains treatment for coal royalties, the metallurgical coal production credit, and refined coal credits; pays a higher excise tax to fund miners' black lung benefits.

industries.industry: Publicly traded partnerships and midstream pipeline operators
industries.note: Loses the corporate tax exemption for fossil-fuel publicly traded partnerships that keeps midstream pipelines out of the corporate tax.

industries.industry: Large banks and asset managers financing fossil projects
industries.note: The bill removes liability caps under the Oil Pollution Act and eliminates the CERCLA lender exemption for large banks and asset managers, making major financial institutions financially responsible for the polluting projects they finance.

industries.industry: Fossil-linked energy technology and carbon capture firms
industries.note: Loses Department of Energy programs, USDA carbon-capture assistance, rural loan guarantees, and the 45Q carbon sequestration credit; faces a restored EPA fee on methane waste emissions.

industries.industry: Renewable electricity and clean hydrogen producers
industries.note: The clean hydrogen credit is rewritten to pay only for hydrogen made with wind, solar, geothermal, marine, or hydropower electricity, shifting federal support toward these producers.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to multiple committees with no hearings, no markup, and no bipartisan cosponsors almost never reach the House floor, and Republicans control every committee of referral and the floor schedule. Unless the political landscape changes, the bill is likely to sit without action for the rest of this Congress.
